subsystems.name: Propellant acquisition
subsystems.role: gathers nitrogen ice from the surface and turns it into gas.

subsystems.name: Storage and pressurisation
subsystems.role: holds propellant between hops as high-pressure gas.

subsystems.name: Propulsion
subsystems.role: provides the ballistic hop and steers the vehicle.

subsystems.name: Power and thermal
subsystems.role: runs the electronics and supplies the heat that gasifies the ice.

subsystems.name: Landing and uprighting
subsystems.role: survives touchdown in low gravity and resets the vehicle for the next hop.

subsystems.name: Guidance and autonomy
subsystems.role: picks safe landing sites without help from Earth.

subsystems.name: Communications
subsystems.role: sends science data back across the outer solar system.

buildSteps.title: Fix the hop budget
buildSteps.detail: Triton's gravity is about 0.08 g, so a 1 km ballistic hop needs only roughly 30 m/s of velocity change — a few percent of escape velocity. That low number is what makes propellant harvested on site enough for a whole mission.

buildSteps.title: Design the collector
buildSteps.detail: Engineers specify a scoop or light drill that can bite into nitrogen ice at about 38 K without welding itself shut, using a trickle of warm gas to loosen the surface.

buildSteps.title: Build the warm section
buildSteps.detail: A radioisotope power source supplies electricity and, more importantly, waste heat. A loop carries that heat to a chamber where the ice sublimes and the gas is warmed and pressurised.

buildSteps.title: Make the thruster
buildSteps.detail: Because the gas is heated nitrogen rather than a chemical propellant, exhaust velocity is modest and the tank must be strong. The nozzle and thrust-vector mechanism are sized for short, powerful impulses.

buildSteps.title: Engineer the lander
buildSteps.detail: Legs, dampers and a self-righting arrangement are designed for a body with almost no atmosphere, where parachutes are useless and every hop ends in a hard, controlled touchdown.

buildSteps.title: Write the autonomy
buildSteps.detail: Round-trip radio time to the Neptune system is several hours, so the vehicle must choose and reach landing sites by itself, using cameras and lidar to avoid crevasses and slopes.

buildSteps.title: Test in a cold vacuum chamber
buildSteps.detail: A full-size unit is exercised in a chamber holding nitrogen ice at Triton-like temperature and pressure, cycling scoop, heater, valve and nozzle many times.

buildSteps.title: Fly a small demonstrator first
buildSteps.detail: A reduced hopper would prove acquisition and hopping on a nearer icy body before a full Triton mission is attempted.

prerequisites.why: the Sun is too faint at 30 AU for solar arrays, and the same unit's waste heat is the mission's energy source.
small hopping robots have moved across a near-Earth asteroid, but nothing has hopped on a body of Triton's size, at its temperature, for years.
landing site selection must happen on board, as it does on recent planetary landers, but not yet in this environment.
valves, bearings and actuators that must work repeatedly for years at nitrogen-ice temperature are unproven.
the ground network already tracks spacecraft at that range, though data rates are low.

pathway.milestone: concept studies of nitrogen-propelled hoppers for Triton, alongside proposed Neptune-system flybys
pathway.unlocks: a defined mission architecture and a list of the technologies it needs.

pathway.milestone: bench and vacuum-chamber demonstrations of ice collection, gasification and repeat hopping
pathway.unlocks: evidence that the propellant cycle closes.

pathway.milestone: a small hopping lander on a nearer icy moon or comet
pathway.unlocks: flight heritage for low-gravity hop guidance and cold mechanisms.

pathway.milestone: a Triton hopper delivered by an orbiter or flyby carrier
pathway.unlocks: sampling many separate terrains, including the plume regions, with one vehicle instead of many landers.
